'''Francis Eugene Low''' (October 27, 1921 – February 16, 2007) was an American [[theoretical physicist]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?lowf |title=Francis Low, Array of Contemporary American Physicists |access-date=2014-08-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305193137/https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?lowf |archive-date=2016-03-05 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was an [[Institute Professor]] at [[MIT]], and served as provost there from 1980 to 1985.
He was a member of the influential [[JASON Defense Advisory Group]].<ref name="weinberg">{{cite web|url=http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/5146.html|title=Oral History Transcript — Dr. Steven Weinberg|date=June 28, 1991|first=Finn|last=Aaserud|publisher=[[American Institute of Physics]]}}</ref>

==Biography==

===Early career===
Low completed a B.S. degree at Harvard in 1942. During the [[Second World War]], he worked on the [[Manhattan Project]].  He was based at what is now the [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]], working on the mathematics of [[uranium enrichment]]. He later entered the [[United States Army]] and served in the [[10th Mountain Division]].

After the war, Low completed his studies at [[Columbia University]], earning a Ph.D. in physics in 1950. He then worked at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], before taking up a faculty position at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign|University of Illinois]].

===Career at MIT===
Low joined the MIT physics faculty in 1957. There his Ph.D. students included [[Alan Guth]],  [[Mitchell Feigenbaum]] and [[Robert K. Logan]].

He was a director of MIT's [[MIT Center for Theoretical Physics|Center for Theoretical Physics]] and the Laboratory for Nuclear Science.

In 1969, Low helped found the [[Union of Concerned Scientists]], and briefly served as its chairman. He stepped down after a disagreement with other members, who refused to consider studying whether [[nuclear reactors]] could be made safe and reliable.

In 1980, Low was appointed provost of MIT.  During his five-year tenure, he was instrumental in bringing the [[Whitehead Institute]] to MIT, and expanded humanities education at the Institute.

Low retired from MIT in 1991, but continued to teach for another few years. His text [https://books.google.com/books?id=Gy45llCaVnAC ''Classical Field Theory: Electromagnetism and Gravitation''] was published in 1997 by [[John Wiley & Sons]].

===Personal life===
In 1948, Low married Natalie Sadigur. Low had a son Peter,<ref>{{cite news|title=Peter Low Wed to Miss Kissin|date=24 April 1983|newspaper=NY Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/04/24/style/peter-low-wed-to-miss-kissin.html}}</ref> two daughters, Julie and Margaret, and six grandsons; he liked to joke that this was statistically improbable. He became a widower in 2003.
